The document provides a rigorous analysis of how this feedback loop leads to model collapse, framing it as a technical constraint on future growth.
key_points.verbatim: If the training data of most future models are also scraped from the web, then they will inevitably train on data produced by their predecessors.

key_points.point: The research employs empirical testing on models like OPT-125m to observe and quantify model collapse, prioritizing observable performance metrics over theoretical speculation. This methodology reflects an accelerationist preference for behavioral and empirical safety, where the focus is on measuring how models actually perform under specific training regimes. By demonstrating that models can still learn some of the underlying task despite degradation, the authors provide a nuanced view of the risks. This approach allows developers to understand the limits of their systems and design better training protocols.

factual_claims.claim: Indiscriminate use of model-generated content in training causes irreversible defects in the resulting models, where tails of the original content distribution disappear.
Training a single moderately large model produces twice the American lifetime's worth of CO2.
The OPT-125m model fine-tuned with real wikitext2 data obtains 34 mean perplexity, compared to a zero-shot baseline of 115.
Training with generated data allows models to adapt to the underlying task, but with performance degradation from 20 to 28 perplexity points in the five-epoch setting.
Preservation of 10% of original training data leads to only minor degradation of performance in recursive training.
Model collapse is a phenomenon observed in generative models trained on recursive synthetic data, characterized by the degradation of model quality over successive generations.
The process of model collapse is inevitable, even in the absence of function estimation error.
